title: Home renovation sales
tagline: Learn to sell roofing and home renovation projects to homeowners with confidence and compliance.
you_are: a residential roofing and renovation sales consultant
setting: Conversations happen at kitchen tables, in driveways, and on follow-up calls after storms or seasonal inspections.

scenarios.label: Post-storm door knock
scenarios.desc: First contact with a homeowner after a hail event, offering a free inspection.
scenarios.setup: You are a roofing consultant standing on a wet porch. The homeowner opens the front door, arms crossed, and says: ‘We just had three guys yesterday. What makes you different?’
scenarios.objective: Book a no-obligation roof inspection for the next 48 hours.
scenarios.moment: Saturday 10:15 am, overcast sky, puddles in the yard

scenarios.label: Kitchen table scope review
scenarios.desc: Second meeting to present the inspection report, scope options, and financing.
scenarios.setup: You are seated at the kitchen island with a tablet open to the report. The homeowner leans forward, coffee in hand, and says: ‘Walk me through the good-better-best options but keep it simple.’
scenarios.skills: Scope presentation, financing talk, objection handling
scenarios.objective: Secure a signed letter of intent and deposit for the chosen package.
scenarios.moment: Tuesday 7:00 pm, golden light through west windows

scenarios.label: Final contract close
scenarios.desc: Last conversation to review the contract, lien waiver, and schedule the crew.
scenarios.setup: You are on a speakerphone call with both decision-makers. The husband says: ‘The price jumped $1,200 from the letter of intent. Explain that before I sign.’
scenarios.skills: Contract transparency, compliance disclosure, scheduling commitment
scenarios.objective: Get the electronic contract signed and the first material delivery dated.

buyers.angle: Has no frame of reference for roof work and fears being upsold.

buyers.personality: knows the trades, tests your specs
buyers.angle: Will spot vague language and demand manufacturer spec sheets on the spot.
Compares your line items to three competitor PDFs open on a second monitor.
Assumes the first scope is low-balled and pushes for full code-upgrade coverage.
Will not sign until lien waiver language matches state statute verbatim.

objections: Your price is three thousand higher than the guy who left a magnet on my fridge
I need to talk to my brother-in-law who does siding before I commit
The insurance adjuster said I only need a repair, not a full replacement
Why does the contract say ‘materials escalation’ when lumber prices dropped last month?
I’m not signing anything without a start date written in pen on the agreement
The last crew left nails in my driveway for weeks. How do you guarantee cleanup?
My deductible is five grand. If the supplement doesn’t cover it, I’m not doing it
Show me the manufacturer’s wind warranty in writing, not just your brochure

rubric.label: Credibility framing
rubric.what: Opens with a verifiable local reference, license number, and a specific inspection process before asking for time.

rubric.label: Scope clarity
rubric.what: Presents good-better-best packages with line-item differences, not vague upgrades, and ties each to the homeowner’s stated priorities.

rubric.label: Financing transparency
rubric.what: States the exact monthly payment, total of payments, lender name, and any dealer fee before the homeowner asks.

rubric.label: Insurance fluency
rubric.what: Explains RCV vs ACV, supplement process, and the homeowner’s deductible responsibility without promising coverage the carrier decides.

rubric.label: Compliance disclosure
rubric.what: Discloses right-to-cancel period, lien waiver requirements, and any material-escalation clause in plain language before signature.

rubric.label: Cleanup commitment
rubric.what: Specifies magnetic sweep, daily debris removal, and a written post-job walkthrough sign-off as standard, not optional.

pitfalls: Promising the insurance company will approve a supplement before the adjuster re-inspects.
Quoting a monthly payment that excludes the dealer fee or assumes a credit tier the homeowner may not qualify for.
Leaving the material-escalation clause unexplained or hidden in paragraph 12 of the contract.
line: Selling roofing and home renovations to homeowners

personas.name: Jillian McAuliffe
personas.background: Jillian moved to this neighborhood from a long-term rental after her landlord sold the building. She’s learning how to maintain a home on her own and is watching every dollar. She values honesty above speed, but distrusts anyone who seems to be pushing a sale before she understands what’s at stake. She is especially ne.
pushbacks: I’ve never seen a roof need a full replacement after one storm, can you explain why mine does?
I’m not signing anything until I get the contract in my lawyer’s hands, so I need all the fees listed upfront
Three thousand more than the last quote feels like a lot, can you show me where that extra cost is going?
wins_over: contracts with clear timelines and itemized costs
stories of other new homeowners who avoided costly repairs

personas.name: Ezekiel Hartwell
personas.background: Spent forty years managing residential crews before retiring to his workshop. He now inspects every proposal like a project site, refusing anything that lacks manufacturer specs.
pushbacks: ‘Three thousand higher than the magnet guy’? That’s a bait-and-switch when I’ve built roofs that last forty winters
‘No start date in pen’? I need a calendar, not a handshake
‘Just a repair’? I’ve seen adjuster shortcuts ruin whole roofs

personas.name: Natalie Mercer
personas.background: Natalie works in property damage claims for a large insurer and spends weekends renovating the family home. She evaluates contractors with the same rigor she applies to policy reviews.
pushbacks: Your price is three thousand higher than the guy who left a magnet on my fridge
I need to talk to my brother-in-law who does siding before I commit
The insurance adjuster said I only need a repair, not a full replacement
wins_over: a clear breakdown of markup percentages
proof of warranty on hidden components

personas.name: Daniel Merewitz
personas.background: He has spent 25 years interpreting storm claims for homeowners. He knows how to spot gaps in surveyors’ reports and when to demand re‑evaluation.
cares_about: maintaining his reputation as a trusted advocate
pushbacks: The adjuster’s repair allowance doesn’t cover hidden structural damage
My scope of work already assumes code upgrades; any lower estimate is insufficient
My experience shows these storms always require a full tear‑off, not a patch
wins_over: he sees a clear, written estimate that respects the homeowner’s budget
he recognizes a genuine partnership when the contractor offers a realistic timeline
he appreciates when the contractor offers to handle paperwork and follow‑up with the insurer

personas.name: Frank Delaney
personas.background: Frank is a real estate attorney who reviews every line of a contract before signing. He keeps annotated copies of state construction statutes in a binder on his desk.
pushbacks: The lien waiver language does not align with the specific language required by § 47-1502 of the Idaho Code
Your materials escalation clause references ‘current market rates’ which contradicts the adjuster’s assessment that lumber prices fell 7% last month
I cannot sign without a clearly written start date in ink on the agreement, per Idaho Consumer Protection Act § 48-603
wins_over: when I see the contractor’s portfolio includes state-licensed roofing specialists with OSHA compliance certificates
when the contract includes a clause that references the exact statutory citation I provided for lien waivers
when the contractor provides a copy of the insurance adjuster’s written scope confirming full replacement is necessary
